text: Israel is beloved in that God surrounded the with mitzvot, tfillin on their heads and arms, and tzizit on their clothes, and mezuzot on their doors.  And somoene who fulfills these three mitzvot, about them it is written "the three-fold cord [shall not be broken]".  Therefore, when a person leaves the through the door of his house, he should kiss the mezuzah. ...

The first blessing is called the forefathers (avot) since we mention the forefathers in it. And one must be very careful to concentrate on the meaning of the words. As from the legal perspective, if one did not have [such] concentration during [this blessing], he must go back and pray [from the beginning]. However in our time, on account of our great iniquities, it is likely that he will not have intention also the second time. Hence we do not go back. Nevertheless, we understand the greatness of the obligation from this. In any event, it appears to me that if one remembered [not having concentrated] before he said, "Blessed are You, Lord," at the end, he should go back and say [the blessing] from "God of Abraham, etc." And on the ten days of repentance, one should say, "Remember us." But if he does not mention [it] and he finishes the blessing, he does not need to go back.

Laws of Handwashing for a Meal and Which Items Require Handwashing (118):
Since hands are busy and touch everything, and in the time when ritual purity and impurity were observed and priests ate terumah, they were required to wash their hands before eating terumah because they were warned not to defile it. Therefore they decreed handwashing even for ordinary hands for terumah. And so that the priests would be accustomed to this, they also decreed for anyone eating bread that it is forbidden to eat until one washes his hands with a quarter-log of water. Anyone who treats handwashing lightly is uprooted from the world, and this commandment aids one who is careful with it, if his other deeds do not prevent it, such that he will become wealthy. And King Solomon of blessed memory and the court established handwashing for a meal.

Five general principles were stated regarding the law of handwashing: (1) which item requires washing; (2) that the vessel be fit for washing; (3) that the water come by human action; (4) that the water be fit for washing; (5) how the washing is performed. We will explain their details. Which item requires washing? They required washing only for bread over which one recites HaMotzi, which is life-sustaining and impossible to live without. But for bread over which one does not recite HaMotzi, such as those over which one recites Borei Minei Mezonot, if one does not establish a meal upon it, handwashing is not required. But when one establishes a meal upon it, and thus it resembles bread and requires the blessing HaMotzi, it also requires handwashing.

For this reason, one who eats bread less than a ke-beitzah (egg-volume), since some say it does not receive ritual impurity, should wash his hands without a blessing due to doubt. For less than a ke-zayit (olive-volume), some say handwashing is not required (Taz and Vilna Gaon), and some say its law is like less than a ke-beitzah (38, Magen Avraham, Eliyah Rabbah). If the bread is secondary to another item, this is explained in Klal 56, section 3.

Something dipped in liquid while still moist, even if one does not touch the place of the liquid, when ritual purity and impurity were observed, handwashing was required by law. But now people have become lenient in this. However, every God-fearing person should be careful in this and wash his hands, but due to doubt should not recite a blessing. Only these seven are called liquids, their mnemonic being YaD SHaCHaT DaM, meaning: wine, blood of animals and birds but not of fish (and this refers to eating for medical reasons in a life-threatening illness), oil, milk, dew, honey, water. Even if one dips only one end, handwashing is required.

Regarding confections fried in honey, it seems to me there is a distinction: if one purchased the honey while still mixed with wax and melted it on that basis in order to fry with it, then it never had the status of liquid and handwashing is not required. But if one purchases honey already separated from the producers, and it is known they separate it to make liquid, handwashing is required even though one fries food in it. So it seems to me. (The Magen Avraham wrote that handwashing is not required, and the Taz wrote that it is required, and in Beit HaLevi, Menachot 31, wrote that since it is congealed it is not a liquid, see there; and see the responsa of Maharit, section 15.)

Fried items that are fried in butter, not only when the butter is congealed, for then the butter has no status as liquid since congealed milk is food and not liquid, but even when the butter is still warm and clear, which is called liquid, even so handwashing is not required. Since butter is food, only when it melts again does it return to being liquid. And since now it comes to prepare food, we maintain that liquid that comes to prepare food is considered food. This applies specifically when the butter did not melt until after the food was placed in it, so that immediately it comes to prepare the food before it became liquid. But if it melted beforehand, it seems to me handwashing is required. See Nishmat Adam.

Regarding brandy mixed with water, according to what I wrote below in the Laws of Passover, section 10, that even if fruits are pickled in it, like cherries and the like, nevertheless it is doubtful whether it is fruit juice (see there), and even if it contains much water (see Magen Avraham Siman 462), therefore fruits pickled in it are doubtful whether handwashing is required. And regarding cooked fruits, since one recites Borei Pri HaEtz on the broth, it does not have the status of liquid (Eliyah Rabbah).

Items that are not customarily touched except to eat with a spoon, such as cooked dishes, do not require handwashing. But what is customarily touched, even if one eats with utensils, this does not help. And even if another person places the food into one's mouth, this does not help, and the eater must wash his hands. But the feeder does not require handwashing (163). It is forbidden to hand a slice to someone one knows has not washed his hands, even if the slice belongs to the eater. And likewise it is forbidden to hand food to someone one knows will not recite the blessing of enjoyment. And certainly regarding heretics it is forbidden to hand them forbidden items or to assist them in anything forbidden to do (Magen Avraham Siman 163 and 247).

Roasted meat—if it was roasted without water, only its own moisture, handwashing is not required. But if there is actual gravy, handwashing is required, for it is like something dipped in liquid. (And what Tosafot, Chullin, entry "ve-ne'ekhalin," wrote: "not required for pot, and were rinsed in fruit juice"—this requires examination, for it clearly implies that gravy is not called liquid. And if not for my hesitancy, it seems to me it should read in Tosafot: alternatively, that were rinsed in fruit juice, meaning one could say regarding roasted food that even roasted requires rinsing; see the Ran and Rashba's commentary. Or one could say that what Tosafot wrote "not required for pot" means like pot-roasted and was cooked without water, only its own gravy; see Magen Avraham Siman 158:10.)
They decreed only regarding the eater, but the drinker, even if he touches liquids, the custom is not to wash his hands.

Laws of Honoring Father and Mother (Yoreh Deah 240):
If one has a father or mother, he should endeavor to attend to their needs, for this is a positive commandment from the Torah and is the most stringent of stringent obligations (as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Peah). A person must honor his father and mother and fear them, and one must be extremely careful in their honor and fear, for their honor and fear are compared to the honor and fear of the Omnipresent, blessed be He. For it is written "Honor the Lord with your wealth," and similarly it is written "Honor your father"; it is written "Fear the Lord your God," and similarly it is written "Each person shall fear his mother and father." There are three partners in a person: the Omnipresent, blessed be He, and his father and mother. Our Sages said: When a person honors his father and mother, the Holy One, blessed be He, says, "I account it as if I dwelled among them and they honored Me." And when one causes pain to his father and mother, the Holy One, blessed be He, says, "It is good that I did not dwell among them, for if I had dwelled among them, they would have caused Me pain." It is obvious that one must love them as his own body, for this is included in "Love your neighbor as yourself." But regarding one's father and mother, their love is compared to love of the Omnipresent, as stated in the Zohar Tetzei: Like a person who strives for his father and mother, loving them more than himself, his soul, spirit, breath, and all his possessions—he considers all of this as nothing when it comes to doing the will of his father and mother. Our Sages said that the entire commandment of "Honor" applies to the father, and [also] to the mother—it is repayment of a debt that the child owes to repay his father and mother for the goodness they bestowed upon him. One who does not honor them is called wicked, as it is written "The wicked borrows and does not repay." And if so, included in this repayment is that he should love them with intense love, just as they loved him, and they should not be a burden or load upon him. If a person does not honor his father and mother, harsh decrees come upon him, as it is written regarding honor of the Omnipresent "Because this people has drawn near with its mouth and honored Me with its lips, but its heart is far from Me...I will continue to astound [them]..." And since He equated their honor with honor of the Omnipresent, then the punishment is also equal. Therefore, just as one who curses God's name is [punished by] stoning, so too one who curses his father or mother is [punished by] stoning (see all this in the Tur and in Sefer Charedim regarding positive commandments dependent on the heart).

Let the mouths of those who speak falsehood be silenced—those who say they need not show gratitude to father and mother, for [their parents] intended only their own pleasure, and the child was born as a result. Since he was born from them, the Holy One Blessed Be He gave nature such that father and mother raise their children, like the nature of every beast, animal, and bird that raise their young, and the children do not show gratitude to their parents. Let them be muted and silenced and shamed, as it is written, "Let lying lips be muted" (Psalms 31:19), for they themselves testify about themselves that they are like animals, and God did not grant them a heart to know and understand. Concerning this the Sages said: "Whoever denies the kindness of his fellow will ultimately deny the kindness of the Holy One Blessed Be He"—for according to their words, they also need not honor and fear the Omnipresent, Blessed Be He. Since we are the work of His hands, it would be fitting [for Him] to be good to and show mercy on His handiwork. There is no doubt that those who say such things are deniers in their hearts.

Honor consists of three dimensions: thought, action, and speech. In thought, as it is written: "He despises a contemptible person, but honors those who fear the Lord" (Psalms 15:4). This means honoring in thought—for if one says that in his heart and eyes they are contemptible, but he honors them only with words, then they are equal in his eyes to himself, since he too is contemptible in his own eyes. Rather, it must mean that he honors them in his heart—that they are important in his eyes and heart. That is, he should imagine in his eyes that they are great and honorable people, even though in the eyes of other people they are not considered important at all. This is the essence of honor—for otherwise, it is written: "With their mouth and lips they honor Me, but their heart is far from Me" (Isaiah 29:13), as I wrote.

In action, how is one obligated to honor them? With his body and with his wealth: to feed them, give them drink, clothe them, and attend to all their needs. As it states in the Mekhilta: "Honor your father" — I might think with words alone. Therefore it says, "Honor the Lord with your wealth" (Proverbs 3:9), thus equating their honor with the honor of the Omnipresent. Now we can conclude: feed them, give them drink, clothe them, bring them in and take them out. And whatever one gives them should be done with a cheerful countenance. For even if one feeds them fattened fowl every day but shows them a grim face, he is punished for it. And conversely, even if one makes them grind at a mill, yet his intention is for their benefit — to save his parents from something harder than this — and he speaks words of appeasement to their hearts, showing them that his intention is for their good and that he cannot provide for them in any other way, until they are appeased to grind, he inherits the World to Come. And one is obligated to serve them as a servant serves his master. (See Kiddushin 31b in Tosafot s.v. "Kabed" and s.v. "VeTordo")

Regarding speech: If one needs something in the city and knows that people will fulfill his request for his father's sake—even though he knows they would also do it for him personally—he should not say "Do such-and-such for me," but rather "Do it for my father," in order to attribute the honor to his father. If he is uncertain about the matter, he has permission to do as he wishes. However, if he knows that his father has enemies in the city, he should not make requests in his father's name, for this would only bring disgrace to his father, since they will not do it for him.

One is obligated to honor him even after his death. If one relates a teaching heard from him, one says: "Thus said my father, my teacher—may I be atonement for his resting place." Similarly, when signing one's name, one signs as "the son of my master." All this applies specifically within twelve months; after twelve months, one says "of blessed memory." Likewise, the Kaddish prayers customarily recited are rooted in the obligation to honor father and mother, for one is obligated to honor them in death.

One is obligated to stand before one's father and mother to their full height. It seems to me that the law is like that of one's primary teacher in section 242, meaning that once he sees them from as far as the eye can see until they are hidden from him or until they sit down, he is only obligated to stand morning and evening, except in the presence of others who do not know that he already stood before them. Some say that even a hundred times a day he is obligated. If they are in an upper story and the son is below on the ground floor, he need not stand before them since they are in a separate domain.

What constitutes fear? He should not stand in the place designated for his father to stand in council with his colleagues to deliberate, because it appears that he considers himself among the counselors and equates himself with his father. He should not stand in the place designated for his father to pray there, nor sit in the place designated for him to sit in his house. Rather, he should stand before him as a servant before his master. He should not contradict his words. If his father disputes with another person, whether regarding a matter of law or other matters, it goes without saying that he should not say "so-and-so's words seem correct," for that contradicts his words, and all the more so he should not say "the truth is not as you say." Rather, even if his father's words seem correct to him, he should not say in his presence "my father's words seem correct," for this is a disgrace to his father as it shows that his opinion is more decisive than his father's opinion. But if he has a response to the disputant's words, he should respond to him—and this specifically in his presence. But not in his presence, it is permitted to say "my father's words seem correct to me," for on the contrary, this is honoring his father. Even to dispute with his father is permitted when not in his presence. However, if there is another who holds the same opinion as his father and he wishes to dispute his father's reasoning, since there is another, he should not mention his father's name but should say the opinion of that other person who holds like his father (Turei Zahav). He should not call him by his name, neither in his lifetime nor after his death, but rather says "my father, my teacher" and "my mother, my teacher." If his father's name was the same as another person's and it is an unusual name that people are not accustomed to, some permit [calling others by that name] when not in his presence. Similarly, if it is a name that many people are accustomed to, such as Abraham, Isaac, etc., and the like, some permit calling others by it even in his presence, and some forbid it in his presence. In any case, nowadays we are lenient about it, for presumably his father forgives.

One whose father's or mother's mind has become disturbed should try to conduct himself with them according to their mental state until they receive mercy [from Heaven]. If it is impossible to endure this, he should go away and appoint others to care for them properly so that they not come to disgrace.

If he saw his father transgress words of Torah, he should not say to him "Father, you have transgressed words of Torah." Rather, he should say to him "Father, thus and thus is written in the Torah," as if asking him, and not as if warning him, and he will understand on his own and not be embarrassed. If he said a teaching in error, he should not say to him "you erred," and even regarding a matter of law, he should not say to him "that does not work."

How far does their fear and honor extend? If the son was dressed in precious garments and sitting at the head of the congregation, and his father and mother came and tore his garments, struck him on his head, and spit in his face—and likewise even if they took his purse of gold coins and threw it before him into the sea—he may not shame them, nor be distressed before them, nor become angry with them. Rather, he should be silent and fear the One who commanded thus. Nevertheless, he may sue them in court that they should pay him for what they damaged. Some say that before they caused him loss, the son may prevent them from causing him loss even though they have means to pay, in order not to go to the trouble of standing in court before a judge. Nevertheless, after they already caused him loss, it is forbidden to shame them, for what has happened has happened. If they do not have means to pay, everyone agrees it is permitted to prevent them from causing him loss, for he is not obligated to honor them except from their own means, as below in section 12. This specifically applies where there is actual monetary loss, but if they wish to remove from him mere profit, it is forbidden for everyone to prevent them and cause them distress. Moreover, even if his father and mother are sleeping and the keys to his son's shop are under their heads, it is forbidden to wake them from their sleep even though he will thereby lose much (Turei Zahav subsection 10). But if profit comes to his father and if he does not wake him he will be more distressed by the loss of profit, it is a commandment to wake him since his father is happy with this. Similarly, when waking him to go to the synagogue or for a matter of a commandment, for everyone is obligated in honoring the Omnipresent (Shulchan Aruch section 337).

Feeding and giving them drink from their own resources if they have them. But if they do not have and the son does, we compel him to support them from his own as a form of charity. Therefore, even though we do not compel fulfillment of the commandment of honoring parents because it is a positive commandment whose reward is stated alongside it—"that your days may be lengthened"—which implies there is no reward in this world except the punishment of not lengthening one's days, nevertheless in this case we compel him, for one's father is no less than any other charity case, since we compel charity giving. It is forbidden to give charity to another poor person, as one's father takes precedence over everyone. If his means allow it and he supports his father from his own charity funds, a curse should come upon him for disgracing his father. If the son has nothing, he need not go begging door-to-door to feed them. However, some authorities hold that only when he has nothing at all need he not go begging to give to his father, but whatever he has he must give to his father even if he will need to go begging. For all agree he is obligated to honor and serve him in matters that do not involve giving his own money. If the son has that day's sustenance, even though this will cause him to neglect his work and tomorrow he will need to go begging, [he must serve his parents]. But if the son does not have that day's sustenance, he is not obligated to neglect his work and go begging or fast that day, and he need not even honor them with his body.

If his father tells him to violate words of Torah, whether a positive or negative commandment, even a rabbinic commandment, he should not listen to him, as it is written "Each person shall fear his mother and father—I am the Lord"—you are all obligated in My honor. Therefore, if they commanded him not to speak with so-and-so and not to forgive him, but the son wishes to make peace immediately, he need not be concerned with his father's instruction, as it is forbidden to hate any person unless one saw him committing a transgression.

If his father says "Give me water" and there is a transient mitzvah before him—if it is possible for the mitzvah to be performed by others, such as burial of the dead, accompanying [the deceased], and the like: if he already began that mitzvah he should complete it, as one engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from other mitzvot. If he has not begun it, he should leave the mitzvah and attend to their needs. If there are no others to do it and the time is passing, he should engage in the mitzvah and leave their honor. If the time for the mitzvah is not passing, he should attend to their honor and afterward perform the mitzvah.

Torah study is greater than honoring father and mother. Therefore, if the son wishes to go to another place to study where he trusts he will see a sign of blessing in his learning, and the father objects fearing he will come to improper conduct there, he need not listen to his father. Similarly, if the father objects to the son marrying a woman he desires, he need not listen to his father. One whose mother told him to do something and then his father came and said "Who told you to do that?" should not say "Mother," even if they curse him, lest his father become angry at his mother.

Honoring father takes precedence over mother in prioritization, since she is obligated to honor her husband. But if she is divorced, they are equal. There is never any distinction in any matter between father and mother.

Both man and woman are obligated in honoring and fearing father and mother, except that if the woman's husband objects she is exempt, but otherwise she is obligated. (It requires examination among the authorities: why is honoring one's father-in-law a Torah obligation? Why would she be exempt, since he too is obligated, as stated above that father precedes mother because she too is obligated to honor her husband?)

A mamzer is obligated to honor his father and mother and to fear them, and even if his father is wicked and a transgressor, he is obligated. Some say that as long as he has not repented, he is not obligated to honor him, but in any case it is forbidden to cause him distress.

Anyone who disgraces his father or mother, even with words, even by hint, is included in the curse from the Almighty, as it says "Cursed is one who degrades his father or mother." And regarding this, Solomon said through divine inspiration in Proverbs: "The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother—the ravens of the valley will pluck it out." He said "obedience to [an aged] mother," meaning to teach that it is common for women's words to be foolish, and especially when she is old, her words are foolish. Therefore, even one who disgraces an aged mother—"obedience" refers to the gathering [of wrinkles], for due to old age wrinkles form in her flesh—even so, his punishment is severe. And it is written in Sefer HaChareidim: "There was an incident in our days of a man who supported his mother, but she was light and despised in his eyes because she had married another man after his father's death. This man traveled by sea and was killed and thrown into the sea. The Jews searched for him and found him on the seashore with one eye gouged out, pecked by the ravens."

It is forbidden for a person to make his yoke heavy upon his children and to be exacting with them regarding his honor, lest he bring them to stumbling. Rather, he should forgive and overlook them, for a father who forgives his honor—his honor is forgiven.

One who strikes his adult son: some say when he is twenty-two years old, and some say twenty-four years old. It seems to me that it all depends on the son's nature, and even younger than this, we excommunicate him, for he transgresses "before the blind [do not place a stumbling block]." Rather, he should rebuke him with words.

A person is obligated to honor his father's wife even though she is not his mother, as long as his father is alive, as it is written "Honor your father"—to include his father's wife. And likewise, he is obligated to honor his mother's husband as long as his mother is alive, as it is written "and your mother"—to include his mother's husband. But after death, he is not obligated in their honor, though it is proper to honor them. And the Sefer Mitzvot Katan writes that during their lifetime the obligation is from the Torah, and after death it is rabbinic.

A person is obligated to honor his older brother, whether he is his brother from his father or from his mother, as it is written "and your mother"—the extra vav [implies additional obligations]. And even if the younger one is greater in Torah than the older one [he must still honor him]. Nevertheless, it is forbidden for the older one to disgrace the younger one, since he is a Torah scholar, one must show respect for the Torah. But if he does not show respect for the Torah, he is not acting properly with him, and [the younger] is not obligated to honor him.

A person is obligated to honor his father-in-law and mother-in-law, for David called Saul "my father," and he was his father-in-law. And he is obligated to honor them as other elders and distinguished people.

A person is obligated to honor his grandfather. Therefore, if his father cannot support his (the father's) father, we compel the grandson to support his grandfather with the same obligation he has toward his father—except that he is more obligated to honor his father than his grandfather.
If the father wishes to serve his son, it is permitted to receive [such service] from him, unless the father is a Torah scholar—for in that case it is forbidden to make use of a Torah scholar.

One who curses his father or mother, even after their death, is liable to stoning if there are witnesses and warning—whether male or female who cursed. This applies specifically when they cursed using God's explicit Names; but if they cursed using a Divine epithet, they are only liable to a negative commandment and receive lashes, as one who curses any Jew.
One who strikes his father or mother and makes a wound is liable to strangulation. Without a wound, it is only a negative commandment, and they receive lashes as one who strikes any Jew.

If there was a thorn stuck in his father, he should not remove it lest he come to make a wound in him. Similarly, if he is a physician, he should not let his blood or amputate his limb even though he intends it for healing. When does this apply? When there is someone else who can do it. But if there is no one else and he is suffering, then he may let his blood and cut [as needed], according to what they permit him to do.

In Tanna D'bei Eliyahu it states: "Honor your father" is juxtaposed to "You shall not commit adultery," to teach you that if a man marries a woman and she does not honor his father and mother, it is as if he commits adultery all his days. [It continues] to "You shall not steal"—that if a person has sons and daughters in his house and they do not honor their father and mother, it is as if he steals souls. (See Sefer HaChareidim from 561 to 585, and from sign 334 to 346.)
Shabbat and Festivals: Roosters and cats and any animal that is commonly found in a home that will likely return to the home in the evening. Even when this animal leaves the home they are considered as if they are trapped and do not have an issue of trapping on Shabbos. Therefore if the animal leaves the home and you don't want it to get stolen and when you grab the animal it is pleasant and you don't have to chase after the animal, you can push it from the back (into the home) .

The laws of Erev Yom Tov apply like those of Erev Shabbat in all respects. It is proper for every person to immerse in a mikveh on Erev Yom Tov, in memory of the Temple, when all Israel were obligated to purify themselves on festivals before appearing there. One cuts hair and trims nails. Anything forbidden to instruct a non-Jew to perform on Erev Shabbat for Shabbat is likewise forbidden on Erev Yom Tov for labors prohibited on Yom Tov.

The custom is not to perform bloodletting on the eve of any festival, for on Erev Shavuot, a demon named Tavuach goes forth, and had Israel not accepted the Torah, he would have slaughtered them for their flesh and their blood. The Rabbis therefore decreed [the prohibition] for all festival eves on account of Erev Shavuot. As for cupping glasses, called bankes or Köpfsetzen, some authorities permit them, except on Hoshana Rabbah, which is a Day of Judgment. In any case, on Erev Shavuot one should be stringent. On the night before a festival, bloodletting is permitted, except for the night of Hoshana Rabbah. The last day of Passover is entirely permitted, as it is not a festival unto itself. (Magen Avraham, Siman 468) All of the above applies when one wishes to let blood for purposes of health. However, where there is danger to life, the matter has already been widely trodden upon, and "God protects the simple" (Psalms 116:6). Even on Erev Shavuot, the Be'er Heitev permitted it when physicians ordered bloodletting in an illness involving mortal danger — for one can say it is specifically their [ancient] form of bloodletting that was prohibited, but not our [modern] form. Therefore, in a case of danger, one should permit it but not otherwise.

The Kiddush of Yom Tov is only rabbinic in origin, yet the laws of Yom Tov Kiddush are in all respects like those of Shabbat Kiddush (Siman 271) — except that on Yom Tov one adds the recitation of Shehecheyanu, both on the first night and on the second night, for the sake of the Yom Tov. Since the second night is observed on account of safeka d'yoma one is therefore obligated to recite Shehecheyanu on the second night as well. If one did not recite it on the first night and remembered on the first day, one recites it at whatever moment one remembers. Similarly, if one did not recite it on the second night, one recites it whenever one remembers, even on the last day of Yom Tov (Magen Avraham, Siman 483). There is no need to place a new fruit before oneself on the second night in order to recite Shehecheyanu, since the obligation stems from doubt (Eliyah Rabbah, cited in Magen Avraham). However, on the second night of Rosh Hashanah, the custom is to place a new fruit before oneself — for since the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered like a single extended day (yoma arichta), some authorities hold that Shehecheyanu is not recited on the second night at all; therefore a new fruit is placed to serve as the basis for the blessing. This differs from the two days of other Diaspora Yom Tovim. Nevertheless, even on Rosh Hashanah, if one has no new fruit available, Shehecheyanu is recited regardless. On Sukkot, one is obligated to recite Shehecheyanu both on account of the Yom Tov and on account of the Sukkah. Therefore, if one was compelled by circumstances or the like and did not eat in the Sukkah on the first night even though one had already recited Shehecheyanu at home the following day, or on any of the seven days of Sukkot, when one enters the Sukkah, one recites Shehecheyanu on account of the Sukkah. However, one who did not eat in the Sukkah on the second night, having already previously recited Shehecheyanu at home, need not recite Shehecheyanu again upon entering the Sukkah — for the single Shehecheyanu recited once on account of the Sukkah is sufficient (see Eliyah Rabbah, Siman 643 and Magen Avraham). Therefore, on the first night of Sukkot, one recites Leishev BaSukkah immediately after Kiddush, and afterwards recites Shehecheyanu — for that Shehecheyanu applies to the Sukkah as well. But on the second night, the Shehecheyanu does not apply to the Sukkah, only to the Yom Tov; therefore one recites Shehecheyanu immediately after Kiddush and afterwards recites Leishev BaSukkah (in accordance with the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch and the Magen Avraham in Siman 661; so too wrote the Eliyah Rabbah there in the name of many great authorities unlike the Rashal, the Taz, and the Magen Avraham there). As for what the Magen Avraham writes at the beginning of Siman 643 that if the Sukkah was newly built, one recites Zeman first and then Sukkah this applies specifically to one who recited the blessing at the time of building (and so too rules the Bach). On the seventh day of Passover, Shehecheyanu is not recited, since the entire festival constitutes a single pilgrimage. But on Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah, Shehecheyanu is recited, since Shemini Atzeret is a festival unto itself.

Laws of Hanukkah
During the Second Temple period, when Antiochus ruled, he issued decrees against Israel, nullified their religion, and did not permit them to engage in Torah and mitzvot. They seized their property and daughters, entered the Temple, broke through it, and defiled what was pure. Israel was greatly distressed and oppressed, until the God of our ancestors had mercy and saved them. The Hasmonean priests overcame and killed them, saved Israel, and established a royal line from the priests. The kingdom of Israel was restored for more than two hundred years until the destruction of the Temple.

When Israel overcame their enemies and destroyed them — it was on the 25th of Kislev — they entered the Temple and found no pure oil except for one flask, sufficient for only one day. They lit the Temple menorah for eight days until they could press olives and obtain pure oil. Because of this, the Sages of that generation established that these eight days, beginning on the 25th of Kislev, should be days of joy and praise, and that candles be lit each evening at the entrance of homes on all eight nights to display and reveal the miracle. These days are called Hanukkah — meaning "they rested on the 25th," for on the 25th they rested from their enemies. Even though the oil miracle lasted only seven days — since there was oil for one day — it was still fitting to establish the 25th (like Purim was established on the day of rest). Since the oil was also found on that day, they established that lighting should also occur on the night preceding it, to publicize the oil miracle as well.

Although we rule that Megillat Taanit was nullified — the text recording all holidays from the Second Temple era that were later annulled after the destruction, when all joy ceased — Hanukkah and Purim were not nullified. Eulogies and fasting are forbidden; work, however, is permitted. Women have the custom not to do work while the candles burn. Some have the custom to prohibit work on the first and last days, similar to Passover and Sukkot — a good custom, not to be treated lightly, as it is something others adopted as forbidden. Women are more stringent than men because the miracle was wrought through a woman — the daughter of Yochanan the High Priest, who was very beautiful. She told the wicked king she would sleep with him, fed him cheese dishes so he would grow thirsty, drink wine, become drunk, and fall asleep — and so it was. She cut off his head and brought it to Jerusalem. When his generals saw their king was dead, they fled. Because the miracle involved a dairy dish, some have the custom to eat dairy foods on Hanukkah in remembrance.

Although fasting is forbidden, one may eulogize a Torah scholar before the bier (see the laws of Rosh Chodesh). One may observe a ta'anit chalom (fast for a troubling dream), but must then observe a compensatory fast, as one who fasts on Shabbat must do. All other fasts are forbidden — even the anniversary of a parent's death. The day before Hanukkah, the 24th of Kislev, is permitted for fasting; we do not decree against it lest one come to fast on Hanukkah itself, since it is not so stringent. Therefore some fast on it in lieu of erev Rosh Chodesh. Eulogies, however, are forbidden even then. Nonetheless, ideally one should not fast on the 24th of Kislev — and certainly, declaring a public fast is forbidden (Siman 686).

Some say there is a degree of mitzvah to expand festive meals on Hanukkah, since during these days the Tabernacle was completed, and because the oppressors defiled the Temple and performed the eight-day dedication (chanukat habayit). Nevertheless, it is not obligatory as a seudat mitzvah. However, when songs of praise are recited at the meal, it becomes a seudat mitzvah.

One must be very careful about lighting Hanukkah candles. Even a poor person supported by charity should borrow or sell a garment in order to light — to publicize the miracle and add praise and thanksgiving to God. Nevertheless, one need only borrow or sell for one candle per night, which is the essential mitzvah (A"R). If one has one candle but no table candle, one should light it for Hanukkah even though one will inevitably benefit from its light (Siman 678, Magen Avraham).

All are obligated in Hanukkah candles — men, women, and minors who have reached the age of education; a father must educate his child, as all were included in the miracle. A blind person — if he has a wife, she lights; or he may contribute a share in someone else's candles. If he has his own home and no wife, he lights with assistance. A woman may light and fulfill the obligation on behalf of even a man.

All oils are valid, even if the oil does not flow well through the wick — even on the Shabbat that falls within Hanukkah. Though such oils are forbidden for Shabbat candles (lest one tilt the lamp), Hanukkah candles — whose light one may not use — are not subject to this decree. The preferred mitzvah is olive oil, as in the Temple miracle. If unavailable, use oils that burn clearly and cleanly, or wax candles. If these are unavailable, use tallow or fat. Wicks invalid for Shabbat are permitted for Hanukkah. The preferred mitzvah is cotton wool or linen threads. Wicks need not be replaced each night — light with them until consumed. Do not use candles made from the wax of idolatrous temples, even if a non-Jew has nullified them, as they are repulsive.

It is a mitzvah to use a metal lamp for hidur mitzvah (beautifying the mitzvah), or glass. If using an earthenware lamp, once lit for one night it becomes "old" and repulsive — one needs a new vessel each night, or must heat the old one over fire.

If one filled a bowl with oil and surrounded it with wicks — if a vessel is placed over it, each wick counts as a separate candle. Without a vessel placed over it, it does not even count for one candle, as it resembles a bonfire. One may light with lamp-holders (lampes) where each is separate, even without a covering vessel. It seems to me the same applies with a partition between candles, provided there is at least a finger's width between them. This is the custom — only a bowl with no separation between the flames is problematic. However, a circular lamp does not constitute hidur mitzvah. When using wax candles, stand them upright — not one high and one low. Do not twist two candles together; even though the light is greater, it resembles a bonfire. Each must be a single candle. Do not place them so close they warm each other, causing them to bend and fall — that would be a failure to fulfill the mitzvah.

A candle with two wicks — two people may not light from it, even on the first night. Since our custom is for each person to add one candle per night, observers would be confused about the count. However, this may apply only to a two-wick candle. With our Hanukkah menorah of eight openings, two people may light — one at each end — since it is obvious two people are lighting; otherwise they would have lit sequentially.

The place of lighting — in Talmudic times, the mitzvah was at the entrance nearest the public domain. If there is a courtyard, at the courtyard entrance. In our time, since we live among other nations, each person lights inside their home. Even with many rooms and many entrances, one lights only in the main living space where one's household activities occur (Siman 671).

The preferred mitzvah is to place it within a handbreadth of the doorway on the left — so the mezuzah is on the right and the Hanukkah candle on the left, surrounding one with mitzvot. If there is no mezuzah, place it on the right, since the right is always preferred. The most preferred placement is in the doorway opening itself, as will be explained in Siman 24 (ibid.).

The mitzvah is to place it more than three handbreadths above the ground and less than ten — at this height it is apparent the candle was placed there for a mitzvah, not for ordinary use. If placed above ten handbreadths, the mitzvah is fulfilled. But if placed above twenty cubits, it is not fulfilled, since above twenty cubits the eye does not perceive it well (ibid.).
If many people must light in various locations, they should be careful not to light where lights burn year-round — there would be no indication of the mitzvah at all (ibid.).

One who lives in an upper story may place the menorah in the window, even above ten handbreadths. It seems to me that for us, a window is preferable to a doorway, since it is visible to those in the public domain. If the window is more than twenty cubits above the floor of the public domain — and thus not visible to passersby — it is better to place it by the entrance (ibid.).

One lights and recites blessings in the synagogue for pirsumei nisa (publicizing the miracle). The menorah is placed on the southern wall; candles are arranged east to west (some arrange them north to south — each community follows its own custom). No one fulfills their obligation through the synagogue candles; one must return home and light again. One lights in the synagogue between Mincha and Ma'ariv. On Erev Shabbat, if close to nightfall with no minyan present, one blesses and lights immediately — there is still pirsumei nisa when people come later. In the synagogue, a mourner should not light on the first night, when the congregation is joyful and recites Shehecheyanu; on other nights a mourner may. But at home, a mourner on the first night does recite Shehecheyanu (Siman 671, Taz).

The time for lighting is at the end of sunset — tzet hakochavim (nightfall) — without delay. If occupied, one may light from plag hamincha onward — an hour and a quarter before nightfall, calculated in seasonal hours — provided enough oil is placed to burn until half an hour after nightfall. If the candle does not remain lit into the night, the mitzvah has not been fulfilled and one must relight with a blessing. It seems to me that if uncertain whether nightfall has arrived, one may light, and one may hasten slightly (see Pri Chadash, Siman 672 and the Vilna Gaon's commentary).

If one forgot or intentionally did not light at sunset, one may continue to light until people have ceased from the marketplace — approximately half an hour after nightfall — as pirsumei nisa still applies. This applied in Talmudic times, when lighting was done outside. Once the marketplace is empty, there is no longer recognition. For us, who light inside, one should ideally light on time. After the fact (be-di'avad), as long as household members are awake, one may light with a blessing. If they have gone to sleep, one lights without a blessing — for just as in their time a blessing was recited only when pirsumei nisa applied, so too for us.

Before lighting, one should gather all household members to publicize the miracle. Once the time arrives, it is forbidden even to study Torah — certainly to eat or converse. Even if one has begun [learning], one stops and prays Ma'ariv first — provided one does not delay past the primary lighting time (until the marketplace is empty). Otherwise, it is better to light first. Some rule one should light before Ma'ariv — and this was the practice of the Vilna Gaon.
Laws of Purim When Adar enters, we increase in joy.

On the Shabbat before Purim, we read Parshat Zachor, and it is a positive commandment from the Torah to remember the deed of Amalek and to hate him with a fixed hatred in the heart, to the point that if it were possible to erase him from the world so that no trace of him would remain—neither man nor beast nor his vessels nor his possessions—so that his name would not be mentioned to say "this is from Amalek," as it is written "Remember what Amalek did... you shall blot out the memory of Amalek." However, some say that this Torah commandment is fulfilled by what we read in this portion during the weekly Torah cycle. Nevertheless, since there is no distinguishing mark here—it being merely the weekly portion—and furthermore, since commandments require intention, therefore they designated to juxtapose the reading of the Amalek portion to the Megillah, since there too is written the destruction of Amalek, as Haman was from the descendants of Amalek. And some say that Parshat Parah is also a Torah commandment to read it, and therefore those who live in settlements that don't have a minyan must come to a place that has a minyan on these Sabbaths to hear these portions. And if it's impossible for them to come, nevertheless they should be careful to read them with melodies and cantillation marks (685).

In the days of Mordechai and Esther, they gathered on the 13th of Adar to fight and stand up for their lives, and they needed to seek mercy and supplications that God would help them take revenge on their enemies. And we find that when they were in a day of war, they would fast, for thus said the Sages that Moses our teacher on the day he fought with Amalek was fasting. And if so, certainly also in the days of Mordechai they were fasting on that day. And therefore all of Israel accepted upon themselves a public fast to fast on the 13th of Adar, and it is called the Fast of Esther, in order to remember that the Creator, blessed be He, sees and hears each person in their time of distress when they fast and return to God with all their heart, as they did in those days. Nevertheless, it is not as obligatory as the four written fasts, and therefore there is leniency for it when necessary, such as for pregnant and nursing women, or even one who is slightly ill from eye pain—if they are suffering greatly they should not fast, and similarly a woman who gave birth within 30 days, and they can make it up later. But the other healthy people should not separate from the community. And if Purim falls on Sunday, they fast on Thursday. And if a circumcision falls on it, it is permitted to eat at the circumcision, and the next day, Friday, those who ate will fast—thus wrote the Rema. But the Taz and Acharonim wrote that it is forbidden to eat on Thursday; rather they should make the meal at night like the law of the 17th of Tammuz. And it seems obvious to me that the baalei brit are permitted to eat on Thursday, as I wrote in Principle 132 regarding the 9th of Av that is postponed, and they don't need to fast on Friday. This is according to the opinion of the Taz who established it specifically on Thursday, and indeed this is implied in the She'iltot, Parashat Tissa. But according to the opinion of the Rema that there is no fixed day here, then all the participants of the meal are permitted to eat in the morning as well, only they are obligated to fast on Friday, and there is no difference between the baalei brit and other people. And apparently the custom is like the Taz, since we did not see making the meal during the day (see Taz section 686).

It is customary to give before Purim half of the established coin in that place and at that time, in remembrance of the half-shekel that they used to give in Adar for the communal offerings. The custom is to give three halves, as in Parashat Ki Tisa it is written three times "terumah" (offering). A minor does not need to give, but some say that from the age of thirteen when he has brought [two pubic] hairs—meaning he is already an adult—he is obligated. And some say that until the age of twenty he is exempt. And any minor whose father gave on his behalf once is obligated to give forever.

A person is obligated to read the Megillah at night and then repeat it during the day, as a remembrance of the miracle — that they cried out day and night. The daytime reading may be done anytime from sunrise until the end of the day, and if one read it from dawn, one has fulfilled the obligation. The nighttime reading begins immediately after the emergence of the stars, and its time extends throughout the night. However, before the emergence of stars, even if one is greatly distressed from the fast, it is forbidden to advance the reading. One who reads before the emergence of stars has not fulfilled the obligation at all, even if he read only part of it before the stars emerged — he must read it again (though the author suggests not repeating the blessing, contrary to other opinions). If there is a great need, or if it is impossible to hear the Megillah before tasting something to strengthen oneself slightly from the weakness of the fast, it is permitted to taste a little, such as drinking coffee and the like.

All mitzvot, even those from the Torah, are postponed for the reading of the Megillah because of publicizing the miracle — unless there is insufficient time to do both. If by reading the Megillah one will not be able to fulfill a Torah-level mitzvah, then since it is a Torah-level obligation and the Megillah is rabbinic, the Torah mitzvah takes precedence, even if this means not reading the Megillah at all. However, for a met mitzvah (abandoned corpse) lying in the field in disgrace, one cancels the Megillah and buries it first, even if there will be no time at all to read the Megillah afterward — for the honor of human beings overrides a rabbinic mitzvah. But for burial of a corpse that is lying in one's home, the Megillah takes precedence, since it is possible to bury it afterward. The custom is to perform circumcision before the Megillah.

Even Torah study, which is equivalent to all the mitzvot, is set aside to hear the Megillah reading in public. Even if one could assemble ten people, it is nonetheless a meritorious mitzvah to go to the synagogue — he, his wife, and his children — to hear the Megillah with a multitude of people. Nevertheless, it seems to the author that one who prays throughout the year regularly in a designated minyan need not go to the main synagogue.

In Mordechai's time, during the miracle, it is written that the Jews everywhere fought on the 13th and rested on the 14th, making it a day of feasting and gladness. In Shushan, the Jews were given permission to fight the gentiles also on the 14th, and they did not celebrate until the 15th. Since in that time it was divided into two days, therefore when Mordechai and Esther, with the agreement of the Men of the Great Assembly, established Purim for generations, they also divided it into two days. It would have been fitting to establish that every city surrounded by a wall like Shushan should be like Shushan and observe it on the 15th, and it would have been fitting to link the honor to Shushan and establish that every city surrounded by a wall from the time of Achashverosh should read on the 15th. But since the Land of Israel was destroyed at that time, they established that every city surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua bin Nun should read on the 15th, and the rest on the 14th — except for Shushan, which even though it was not walled from Joshua's time, nevertheless reads on the 15th because the miracle occurred there. Therefore, every city that we know was surrounded by a wall from Joshua's time observes it on the 15th, even if it is not walled now, and even if they are outside of Israel. Even villages adjacent to them within a mil, even if they are not visible, or if they are visible even if not adjacent, read on the 15th. If there was doubt whether it was walled from Joshua's time or not, they read on the 14th and 15th at night, but they only recite blessings on the reading on the night of the 14th and its day. This is the custom in Prague. Since in our country there is no doubt at all about this in any city, the author did not elaborate on this.

Originally, villagers who supplied city needs on Purim could read early (11th, 12th, or 13th of Adar) when they came to town on Monday/Thursday for Torah reading. Today, one traveling at sea who won't have a Megillah on Purim may read on these days without a blessing. If that's impossible, he may read from Rosh Chodesh onward (since the whole month turned to joy). If a Megillah becomes available on the 14th, he reads again with a blessing, even if he read on the 13th. On the 15th he likely needn't repeat it, but if he didn't read at all, he reads on the 15th without a blessing. After the 15th there is no time at all. Anyone reading outside the fixed time needn't have ten people.

The Megillah isn't read on Shabbat—even walled cities advance to Friday—lest one carry it four cubits in the public domain. On that Shabbat it's forbidden even to move the Megillah. But when the 13th falls on Shabbat, the Megillah may be moved. Still, one shouldn't bring it to synagogue even with an eruv, since it's preparation from Shabbat to weekdayEveryone is obligated: men, women, converts, slaves (even unemancipated). Children should be trained. One fulfills the obligation by hearing a reader, provided the reader is himself obligated. A deaf-mute reader doesn't discharge listeners. Women are obligated to hear, not to read; a man should read for them. However, if no man is available, a woman may read for herself from a valid Megillah with the blessing "to hear the reading of the Megillah." Each person should read at home for his maidservants and daughters.

The ideal is to hear in synagogue with many people. At minimum, ten adult men should be present for publicizing the miracle. Whether women count toward ten is uncertain. If ten aren't available, one reads individually—there's still publicity elsewhere. If the city already had a public reading, an individual may read alone le-chatchilah.
§13: Without a Minyan

If there's no minyan and all know how to read, each reads for himself (the reader doesn't discharge others with fewer than ten). Be-di'avad, if one read intending to discharge listeners, they fulfill their obligation. Some say even le-chatchilah one person should read for the others. If only one knows how to read, he certainly reads for everyone.
§14: Kashrut of the Megillah

The Megillah is called a "book" and must be written on parchment according to Torah-scroll laws (detailed in §698). It must be sewn with sinews; linen thread invalidates it. If no sinews are available, one may sew part with thread. Vowel points or cantillation marks shouldn't be added, but be-di'avad it's valid; le-chatchilah they're permitted if no one knows how to read properly. Reading without cantillation is permitted if words are pronounced correctly (past/future verb forms mustn't be switched). If one reads "Yehudayim" (dual) instead of "Yehudim," it's valid since the meaning doesn't change. One may recite a blessing on all these. But if the Megillah is written/printed on paper or in our printed books, even if it's the only one in town, one doesn't fulfill the mitzvah and certainly doesn't bless. A stolen Megillah: obviously no blessing, but be-di'avad if read, one fulfills the obligation (there's no theft in sound).
§15: Standing or Sitting

Public reading shouldn't be done sitting, out of respect for the congregation. An individual may read sitting or standing. Two may read simultaneously—though normally two voices aren't audible, with the Megillah, because it's beloved, people concentrate to hear.
§16: Reading from the Written Text

It must all be read from the written text; reading by heart doesn't fulfill the obligation. Le-chatchilah the entire text must be before him, complete to the last letter. Be-di'avad, even if several words were missing and read by heart, one fulfills the obligation. Some say if the missing words don't invalidate the reading, one fulfills the obligation even without reading them at all, but with words that invalidate (e.g., "the days of Purim will not pass"—omitting "not"; "gifts to the poor"—omitting the mem), everyone agrees one doesn't fulfill it. Since not everyone knows what invalidates, and some say one always repeats, therefore one always repeats even if one letter was skipped, without a blessing. If one knows it invalidates, repeat with a blessing. If one read "Mordechai sat" (past) or "Haman fell" (past) instead of present forms, even after finishing the entire Megillah, one must reread without a blessing. If an entire passage is missing, even in the middle, or if the beginning or end is missing even if not a complete passage, one doesn't fulfill even be-di'avad. Same if letters are too blurred to be recognizable in most of it, or if letters are broken.
§17: Holding an Invalid Text

One holding an invalid Megillah or our printed Chumash shouldn't read along with the reader—he might concentrate on his own reading, rendering it like reading by heart. Even if he intends to concentrate on the reader's words, we worry another might hear his reading and intend to fulfill through him. Therefore no one should assist the reader orally. The verses the congregation recites aloud must be repeated by the reader from the valid Megillah.
§18: Not Interrupting

One mustn't interrupt the reading or delay between parts; read it continuously. Certainly talking is forbidden. Be-di'avad, even if one spoke, or paused an hour or more then returned to where he stopped and finished, he fulfills the obligation—provided the reader spoke (he still read it all). But if the listener spoke and didn't hear even one word, as explained in §16, he must repeat. If the reader was drowsy, he fulfills it (he still read). But a drowsy listener doesn't fulfill it.
§19: Skipping

If one read and skipped a word or verse, even though he finished everything else, the remedy isn't to read the skipped part afterward. Rather, he must begin from that skipped word and read in order. Otherwise he doesn't fulfill.
§20-21: Understanding & Intention

Women, slaves, or one who doesn't understand Hebrew—even though they don't know or understand at all—still fulfill, since there's at least the mitzvah of reading and publicizing the miracle. The reader must intend to discharge all listeners, and the listener must intend to fulfill. One must hear the entire Megillah; if he missed even one word, he repeats (as above). But if he didn't concentrate on every word, he fulfills—it's no worse than women and slaves.

Whoever has had a miracle occur for them, and all the more so the inhabitants of a city, can establish, by popular agreement, for themselves and those who come after them to make that day into a “Purim”. And it seems to me that the meal which they make to commemorate the miracle is considered at the level of a seudat mitzvah [meal with halachic weight] ... So, too, do we practice regarding the miracle which was performed for us in the year 5564, the night of the 16th of Kislev.  There was death in the courtyard in which I live because of a conflagration which started from gunpowder. Several houses in the courtyard fell, including one house that was mine.  In the room where my whole family was located, two half-walls and one beam fell ... Not a single one (i.e. member of the family) did not shed at least some drops of blood. G-d in His mercy and kindness considered for us the blood like a sacrifice to atone, and saved us, and all of us remained alive. Even though I suffered a great loss of several hundred adumim (a currency), G-d in His kindness substituted blood for money [lit. damim for damim]. Aside from us, there were killed, in our many sins, in my courtyard, 31 people ... And in order to tell of the wonders of G-d, as it is written (Tehillim 111:4) “He created a memorial for His wonders”, I have   accepted upon myself and my descendants, without vowing, on the 16th of Kislev, since in our land it is already a day of fasting in many communities for the chevra Kadisha who do kindness, to devote at  least half of it for G-d, and whoever can  should  fast. And on the following night, immediately after Maariv they should gather and light candles like on Yom Tov and sing the Shir HaYichud slowly and pleasantly, and the Shir HaKavod with song, and afterwards [recite] chapters of Psalms slowly ... And after this to make a meal for those who learn Torah and to give charity in accordance with the blessing of G-d, as much as one can afford.
